title: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: we have arrived at the conclusion, as regards unicellular organisms, that not only their general configuration but also _their departures from symmetry_ may be correlated with the molecular forces manifested in their fluid or semi-fluid surfaces.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VI, “A Note on Adsorption”; topic “Cell form and molecular forces”. Scope: unicellular organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch06-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.47

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shape asymmetry is measurable, but the causal statement is underspecified and risks becoming compatible with nearly any cellular mechanism. Existing imaging can test narrow modern interpretations, not the full generalization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate measured local cortical tension or its perturbation to quantified asymmetry across unicellular organisms and compare predictive performance with cytoskeletal and polarity models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Molecular forces' is broad enough to encompass many rival mechanisms.

Tension is usually inferred rather than measured.

operationalizability: 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Image archives cover a wide range of unicellular outlines, so a restricted geometric reading can be tried on mineralized and a few imaged protists. The claim that those departures from symmetry are produced by local surface tension does not specify a result that would rule out other cortical forces. That gap in discriminating power, not a lack of photographs, is what keeps the claim only partly testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For unicells with a measured asymmetry, test whether the outline matches a surface whose local curvature corresponds to a localized change in surface tension, against a cytoskeletal template that survives membrane extraction. A curvature field that accounts for the asymmetry, and that disappears when cortical mechanics are altered, would support the claim; asymmetries that persist as patterned cytoskeleton with no curvature match would limit it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Almost any outline can be assigned a local tension after the fact, so a mere correlation is a weak decision rule.

Tension is rarely measured on the same cells whose shapes fill the taxonomic image libraries.
